A sine curve, or sinusoid, is the geometric wave shape traced by the sine function, y equals sine of x. It's a smooth, continuous, periodic wave that oscillates symmetrically between its peaks and troughs. Sine curves are foundational in trigonometry and physics, representing simple harmonic motion, sound waves, alternating current electricity, and electromagnetic radiation. The standard mathematical equation is y equals A times sine of B times x minus C plus D, where A is the amplitude, two pi over B is the period, C is the phase shift, and D is the vertical shift. The basic curve y equals sine of x has a period of two pi, an amplitude of one, and passes through the origin with a slope of one. The sine curve is an odd function, meaning it's symmetric under a one hundred eighty degree rotation about the origin. This satisfies the property that sine of negative x equals negative sine of x. In physics, any system undergoing simple harmonic motion—like an idealized pendulum or a mass on a spring—traces out a sine curve over time. Fourier's theorem states that any periodic wave can be decomposed into a sum of sine curves of different frequencies and amplitudes. The derivative of a sine curve is a shifted version of itself, a cosine curve. The derivative of sine of x is cosine of x.
